India receives more remittances than any other country. And the diaspora carries India's soft power. Your turn. Why the ninth of January?

en.title: How long you look back changes the jobless rate

quiz.q: Current weekly status measures activity over:
quiz.why: Right. A reference week of 7 days.

en.transcript: Were you unemployed last week? Or last year? The answer changes India's jobless rate. Usual status asks what you mostly did over the past year. Current weekly status asks about just the past seven days. The Periodic Labour Force Survey began in 2017. It replaced the older five-yearly employment surveys of the N-S-S-O. Labour force participation counts those working or looking for work. The unemployment rate is the share of that labour force without work. Your turn. What period does current weekly status cover?

en.title: In the GST Council, neither side can win alone

quiz.q: In the GST Council, the Centre's vote carries a weight of:
quiz.why: Right. One-third; all the states together have two-thirds.

en.transcript: GST replaced a tangle of central and state taxes. And it created a council where neither side can win alone. The hundred-and-first amendment came in 2016. GST began on the first of July, 2017. The Union Finance Minister chairs the GST Council. Every state's finance minister sits on it. A decision needs a three-quarter majority of weighted votes. The Centre's vote counts for one-third, the states' for two-thirds. So neither can pass anything alone. Your turn. How much does the Centre's vote weigh?

en.title: MSP is announced for 22 crops

quiz.q: MSP is recommended by:
quiz.why: Right. The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices.

en.transcript: Before sowing, the government announces a floor price for many crops. That's the Minimum Support Price. MSP is announced for 22 mandated crops, and a fair price for sugarcane is set separately. The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices recommends it. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs decides. Since 2018–19, MSP has been set at least one and a half times paid-out costs plus family labour. Farmer groups ask for a wider cost measure, C two. Your turn. Who recommends MSP?

en.title: A crisis in 1991 opened India's economy

quiz.q: The 1991 crisis was mainly a:
quiz.why: Right. A balance of payments crisis.

en.transcript: In 1991, India nearly ran out of foreign exchange. What followed changed the economy for good. Foreign exchange reserves fell to just a few weeks of imports. India pledged gold abroad to borrow. The new industrial policy came on the twenty-fourth of July, 1991, the same day as the Union Budget. Liberalisation ended licensing for most industries. Privatisation shrank the public sector. And globalisation cut tariffs and opened the door to foreign investment. Your turn. What kind of crisis was it?

en.title: India landed near the Moon's south pole first

quiz.q: Chandrayaan-3's rover was called:
quiz.why: Right. Pragyan was the rover; Vikram the lander.

en.transcript: On the twenty-third of August 2023, India landed on the Moon. Near its south pole, where no one had landed before. Chandrayaan-1 in 2008 helped find signs of water on the Moon. Chandrayaan-2's lander crashed in 2019. Chandrayaan-3 landed in 2023. The lander was called Vikram. And the rover, Pragyan. India became the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon, and the twenty-third of August is now National Space Day. Your turn. What was the rover called?

en.title: Big projects must be judged before they're built

quiz.q: The EIA Notification, 2006 was issued under:
quiz.why: Right. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

en.transcript: Before a dam, a mine or a highway is built, its effect on the environment must be assessed. That's E-I-A. Category A projects are cleared by the Union environment ministry. Category B projects by state-level authorities. Screening and scoping decide what must be studied. Then public consultation, and an expert appraisal. The notification comes under the Environment Protection Act of 1986, passed after the Bhopal gas tragedy. Your turn. Under which law?

en.title: Thirteen countries take turns naming cyclones

quiz.q: Cyclones in the north Indian Ocean are named from a list kept by:
quiz.why: Right. IMD's Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre, New Delhi.

en.transcript: Biparjoy, Mocha, Tauktae. Who picks the names of cyclones in our region? Thirteen countries around the north Indian Ocean contribute names. In 2020, a new list of 169 names was released, thirteen from each. India's weather department runs the regional centre in New Delhi that names cyclones in this basin. Names must be short, neutral and easy to say. And each name is used only once. Your turn. Who keeps the list?

en.title: Dirty money is washed in three steps

quiz.q: Which stage hides the money's origin through many transactions?
quiz.why: Right. Layering.

en.transcript: How does illegal money become clean? In three steps. Placement puts the cash into the system. Layering hides the trail. Integration brings it back, looking legal. The Prevention of Money Laundering Act was passed in 2002, and came into force in 2005. The Enforcement Directorate investigates under it. The Financial Action Task Force was set up by the G7 in 1989. India became a member in 2010. Your turn. Which stage hides the trail?

en.title: Law is the floor, ethics is the ceiling

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the link between law and ethics?
quiz.why: Right. Law is often called the minimum of ethics.

en.transcript: Is something right just because it's legal? Ethics asks a bigger question than the law does. Law tells you the minimum you must do. Ethics asks what is right, even where the law is silent. Look at the intention behind an act, and the means used. And at its consequences, for everyone affected. Gandhi held that good ends never justify bad means. He said the means are like a seed, and the end, the tree. Your turn. How are law and ethics linked?

en.title: The GS4 syllabus lists the values it wants to see

quiz.q: A civil servant serves every government equally, whichever party is in power. This is:
quiz.why: Right. Non-partisanship.

en.transcript: GS4 tells you exactly which values it is looking for. They're written into the syllabus. Integrity, impartiality, non-partisanship. Objectivity, and dedication to public service. And empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections. Impartiality means being fair to every citizen. Non-partisanship means staying neutral between parties, whoever is in power. Don't just name a value. Show what it looks like in a decision, in one line. Your turn. Which value is this?

en.title: Emotional intelligence has five parts

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Goleman's five components?
quiz.why: Right. IQ is a separate measure; EI's five are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.

en.transcript: Two officers know the rules equally well. Why does one handle a crisis better? Often, emotional intelligence. The term was popularised by the psychologist Daniel Goleman, in his 1995 book, Emotional Intelligence. Self-awareness and self-regulation: knowing and managing your own emotions. Motivation from within. Then empathy, and social skills: reading and handling others. In a tense crowd, or a hard meeting, a calm officer lowers the temperature. That's E-I at work. Your turn. Which one is not a component?

en.title: Gandhi listed seven social sins

quiz.q: Which is one of Gandhi's seven social sins?
quiz.why: Right. Wealth without work.

en.transcript: In 1925, Gandhi published a list of seven social sins. Each one is a thing without its conscience. Wealth without work. Pleasure without conscience. Knowledge without character. Commerce without morality. Science without humanity. Religion without sacrifice. And politics without principle. They make strong openers in GS4 and essays. Pair one with a modern case. Commerce without morality, and a corporate fraud. Kant: treat people as ends, never only as means. Aristotle: virtue is the mean between extremes. Your turn. Which one is on the list?

en.title: Seven principles of public life, from Britain to your answer sheet

quiz.q: The Nolan Principles were first set out in:
quiz.why: Right. 1995.

en.transcript: In 1995, a British committee wrote seven principles for anyone in public office. They're a favourite in GS4. They came from the Committee on Standards in Public Life, chaired by Lord Nolan, in 1995. Selflessness, integrity, objectivity. Accountability and openness. Honesty, and leadership. Probity means integrity that shows. In the files, the money, and the decisions. Your turn. When were they set out?

en.title: A GS4 case study has a shape

quiz.q: In a GS4 case study, the best final option is usually:
quiz.why: Right. It must hold up ethically, legally and in practice.

en.transcript: GS4 case studies have no single right answer. But a good answer has a clear shape. List the stakeholders, and the values that clash. Weigh two or three options. Then choose one, and justify it. Your choice should be ethical, legal and practical. Heroic but illegal is not a good answer. Don't just inform your seniors and stop. And don't preach. Show what you would actually do. Your turn. What should the final option be?

en.title: Two essays, one from each section

quiz.q: How many essays do you write in the Essay paper?
quiz.why: Right. Two, one from each section.

en.transcript: The Essay paper carries 250 marks. And it's the paper most people practise least. You write 2 essays, one from each of two sections. For 250 marks, in three hours. Open with a story, a fact, or a question. Then cover many angles. And close on a balanced, forward-looking note. Spend the first twenty to thirty minutes planning each one. A planned essay rarely loses its way. Your turn. How many essays?

en.title: 150 words for 10 marks, 250 for 15

quiz.q: About how many words does a 15-mark GS answer ask for?
quiz.why: Right. About 250 words.

en.transcript: A Mains answer has to fit a word limit. And the limit tells you how deep to go. A ten-mark question asks for about 150 words. A fifteen-marker, about 250. Two lines of introduction. A body of clear points, with examples. And a short way forward to close. Read the directive word first. Discuss, examine, critically analyse. Each wants a different answer. Your turn. How many words for fifteen marks?

en.title: Ashoka's edicts were unreadable until 1837

quiz.q: Who deciphered the Brahmi script?
quiz.why: Right. James Prinsep, 1837.

en.transcript: Ashoka's inscriptions stood for two thousand years. No one could read them, until 1837. In 1837, James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script. Suddenly, Ashoka's edicts could speak. Archaeological sources include inscriptions and coins, monuments, and excavated sites. Literary sources include Indian texts, from the Vedas to Sangam poetry. And accounts by visitors like Megasthenes, Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang and Al-Biruni. Your turn. Who deciphered Brahmi?

en.title: Painted shelters and the first farms

quiz.q: Microliths are typical of the:
quiz.why: Right. The Mesolithic.

en.transcript: Long before cities, people painted on rock walls in central India. And farmed at Mehrgarh, near the Bolan Pass. The rock shelters of Bhimbetka hold paintings from the Mesolithic onwards. They became a World Heritage Site in 2003. Mehrgarh shows some of the earliest farming and herding in South Asia, from about 7000 BCE. The Palaeolithic, with large stone tools. The Mesolithic, with tiny microliths. The Neolithic, with farming and polished tools. Your turn. Which age?

en.title: Two digs a year apart revealed a lost civilisation

quiz.q: Who first excavated Mohenjo-daro?
quiz.why: Right. R. D. Banerji, 1922.

en.transcript: In the early 1920s, two excavations changed Indian history. They pushed it back by two thousand years. Daya Ram Sahni dug at Harappa in 1921. R. D. Banerji, at Mohenjo-daro, in 1922. John Marshall announced a new civilisation in 1924. Planned towns with grids and covered drains. Standard bricks and weights. And the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro. One mystery remains: the Indus script still hasn't been deciphered. Your turn. Who excavated Mohenjo-daro?

en.title: Big stones marked the dead in south India

quiz.q: Megalithic burials in south India are commonly associated with:
quiz.why: Right. Iron objects and black-and-red ware.

en.transcript: Across south India, large stones mark ancient graves. They're called megaliths. Megaliths are stone burials: cists, dolmens and stone circles. Often with iron tools and black-and-red pottery. Brahmagiri in Karnataka, and Adichanallur in Tamil Nadu. The topic also covers pastoral and farming communities that grew far from the Indus. Your turn. What are they associated with?

en.title: The Rigveda has ten books and 1,028 hymns

quiz.q: How many mandalas does the Rigveda have?
quiz.why: Right. Ten.

en.transcript: The oldest Indian text is the Rigveda. It's mostly hymns to gods of nature. It has 10 books, called mandalas, with 1,028 hymns. Early Vedic society was mostly pastoral, with assemblies like the sabha and samiti. Later Vedic society farmed with iron, and kings grew stronger. The main gods were Indra, Agni and Varuna. Your turn. How many mandalas?

en.title: Sixteen kingdoms, and Magadha won

quiz.q: Which mahajanapada grew into the first great empire?
quiz.why: Right. Magadha.

en.transcript: Around the sixth century BCE, sixteen big states covered north India. One of them would build an empire. Buddhist texts like the Anguttara Nikaya list 16 mahajanapadas. Some ruled by kings, some by assemblies. Magadha had iron ore nearby, and fertile plains. Elephants from the forests, and rivers for transport. The same age saw Buddhism and Jainism. Your turn. Which one?

en.title: A war made Ashoka turn to dhamma

quiz.q: Ashoka describes his remorse over Kalinga in:
quiz.why: Right. Major Rock Edict XIII.

en.transcript: Ashoka's Kalinga war killed and displaced many thousands. His own edict says he regretted it. Chandragupta Maurya came to power around 321 BCE. Ashoka fought Kalinga around 261 BCE. In Rock Edict thirteen, Ashoka records his remorse. After that, he spread dhamma: tolerance, non-violence, care for all. Other sources: Kautilya's Arthashastra, and Megasthenes's Indica. Your turn. Which edict?

en.title: India's national calendar starts in 78 CE

quiz.q: Gandhara art is known for:
quiz.why: Right. Greco-Roman influence.

en.transcript: India's national calendar, the Saka era, begins in 78 CE. Often linked to the Kushana king Kanishka. The Saka era begins in 78 CE, often associated with Kanishka's accession. Gandhara art shows Greco-Roman influence, in grey stone. Mathura art is Indian in style, in red sandstone. The Fourth Buddhist Council met in Kashmir under Kanishka. And Silk Road trade boomed. Your turn. What is Gandhara art known for?

en.title: Three crowned kings ruled the Tamil south

quiz.q: The Hathigumpha inscription belongs to:
quiz.why: Right. Kharavela of Kalinga.

en.transcript: Tamil poems from the early centuries CE describe a world of kings, poets and traders. The Sangam age. The Cheras on the Kerala coast. The Cholas in the Kaveri delta. And the Pandyas, around Madurai. The Tolkappiyam, a work of grammar. And akam and puram poems, on love and war. The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan. In Kalinga, King Kharavela left the Hathigumpha inscription. Your turn. Whose inscription?

en.title: The Gupta age gave us Aryabhata and Kalidasa

quiz.q: The Allahabad Pillar inscription praising Samudragupta was composed by:
quiz.why: Right. Harisena.

en.transcript: Why is the Gupta age called classical? Because of its science, literature and art. Samudragupta's conquests are praised on the Allahabad pillar, written by Harisena. Fa-Hien visited under Chandragupta the second. Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya around 499 CE. He argued the Earth rotates on its axis. Later, Harsha ruled from Kannauj. The Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang wrote about his court. Your turn. Who composed it?

en.title: A southern king stopped Harsha on the Narmada

quiz.q: The Aihole inscription was composed by:
quiz.why: Right. Ravikirti.

en.transcript: Harsha ruled the north. But in the south, the Chalukya king Pulakeshin the second stopped him. The Aihole inscription of 634 CE, by the poet Ravikirti, records Pulakeshin's victory over Harsha. The Pallavas built the rock-cut rathas at Mahabalipuram, and the Shore Temple. The Chalukyas built temples at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal. Your turn. Who composed it?

en.title: Ajanta's paintings span 700 years

quiz.q: Ajanta's murals mainly show:
quiz.why: Right. Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives.

en.transcript: The Ajanta caves were carved into a horseshoe-shaped cliff. Over several centuries. The early caves date from around the second century BCE. The later ones, from the fifth century CE, under the Vakatakas. Prayer halls and monasteries, with murals of Jataka stories. Ajanta became a World Heritage Site in 1983, along with nearby Ellora. Your turn. What do the murals show?

en.title: Three dynasties fought for Kannauj

quiz.q: Which was NOT part of the tripartite struggle?
quiz.why: Right. The Cholas were not part of it.

en.transcript: After Harsha, one city became the prize of north India. Kannauj. The Palas of Bengal, the Gurjara-Pratiharas of the west, and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan, all fought over Kannauj. It controlled the Ganga valley, and carried the prestige of Harsha's capital. This era also saw the rise of Rajput clans, and the Chola navy in the south. Your turn. Which one wasn't?

en.title: Bhakti began with Tamil poet-saints

quiz.q: The Nayanars were devotees of:
quiz.why: Right. Shiva.

en.transcript: Devotional bhakti began in the Tamil country. With saints who sang in the people's language. The Alvars sang to Vishnu. The Nayanars, to Shiva. Shankaracharya taught Advaita, non-dualism, in the eighth century. Ramanuja taught qualified non-dualism, later. Bhakti put devotion above ritual, and welcomed women and lower castes. Your turn. Who did the Nayanars worship?

en.title: Two battles at Tarain opened the way to Delhi

quiz.q: The Second Battle of Tarain was fought in:
quiz.why: Right. 1192.

en.transcript: Prithviraj Chauhan won the first battle of Tarain. He lost the second, a year later. Prithviraj won at Tarain in 1191. Muhammad Ghori won in 1192. In 1206, Qutbuddin Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate. Iltutmish consolidated it with the iqta system of revenue assignments, and the group of forty nobles. His daughter Raziya was the first woman to rule from Delhi's throne. Your turn. When was the second battle?

en.title: Two sultans, two bold experiments

quiz.q: Who shifted the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad?
quiz.why: Right. Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

en.transcript: One sultan controlled market prices. Another moved his capital and minted token coins. Alauddin Khalji fixed prices in Delhi's markets, and measured land to raise revenue. Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted his capital to Daulatabad. And tried token copper coins, which were easily forged. Firoz Shah Tughlaq built canals and new towns. Your turn. Who moved the capital?

en.title: A poet and a saint shaped Delhi's culture

quiz.q: Nizamuddin Auliya belonged to the:
quiz.why: Right. The Chishti order.

en.transcript: In fourteenth-century Delhi, a Sufi saint and a poet were close friends. Nizamuddin Auliya and Amir Khusrau. The Chishti order spread from Ajmer, and Nizamuddin Auliya led it in Delhi. The Suhrawardi order was based in Multan. Amir Khusrau wrote in Persian and Hindavi, and is linked to the qawwali tradition. The economy rested on iqtas, and growing towns and trade. Your turn. Which order?

en.title: A city of victory, sacked in 1565

quiz.q: The Battle of Talikota was fought in:
quiz.why: Right. 1565.

en.transcript: Vijayanagara, the city of victory, was founded in 1336. Its ruins at Hampi are still vast. Harihara and Bukka founded it in 1336. The Bahmani kingdom rose in 1347. In 1565, the Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota. Krishnadeva Raya was its greatest king, and a poet himself. The ruins at Hampi are a World Heritage Site. Your turn. When was Talikota?

en.title: Kabir and Nanak rejected ritual for devotion

quiz.q: Guru Nanak was born in:
quiz.why: Right. 1469.

en.transcript: In the fifteenth century, poet-saints questioned both temple and mosque. They sang of a formless God. Kabir, the weaver-poet of Banaras. And Guru Nanak, born in 1469, the founder of Sikhism. Others worshipped God in form: Chaitanya in Bengal, and Mirabai in Rajasthan. They used local languages, and challenged caste and ritual. Your turn. When was Guru Nanak born?

en.title: Akbar ruled through ranks and tolerance

quiz.q: In the mansabdari system, 'sawar' referred to:
quiz.why: Right. The cavalry a mansabdar had to maintain.

en.transcript: Akbar came to the throne as a boy of thirteen. He built the Mughal state's lasting structure. The Second Battle of Panipat in 1556 secured his throne. He opened the Ibadat Khana for religious debate in 1575, and began the Din-i-Ilahi around 1582. The mansabdari system ranked nobles by zat and sawar. Sulh-i-kul meant peace with all faiths. His revenue system, the dahsala, was shaped by Raja Todar Mal. Your turn. What did sawar mean?

en.title: The empire's widest reach, and its strain

quiz.q: Shivaji was crowned in:
quiz.why: Right. 1674, at Raigad.

en.transcript: Under Aurangzeb, the Mughal empire was at its largest. It was also under great strain. Aurangzeb took the throne in 1658. Shivaji was crowned at Raigad in 1674. Aurangzeb died in 1707, still at war in the Deccan. Long wars in the Deccan drained the treasury. And there was not enough land to pay all the nobles. Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan, art and architecture peaked. Your turn. When was Shivaji crowned?

en.title: Europeans came for spices and stayed

quiz.q: The English East India Company received its charter in:
quiz.why: Right. 31 December 1600.

en.transcript: In 1498, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut. A century later, trading companies followed. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. The English East India Company was chartered in 1600, and the Dutch company in 1602. They bought Indian textiles, spices and indigo, paying largely in silver. Revenue was collected in cash, which tied villages to markets and towns. Your turn. When was it chartered?

en.title: Mughal culture wrote, painted and built

quiz.q: The Akbarnama was written by:
quiz.why: Right. Abul Fazl.

en.transcript: The Mughals recorded their reigns in illustrated histories. And built some of the world's most famous monuments. Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama. Babur wrote his own memoir, the Baburnama, in Turki. Work on the Taj Mahal began around 1632, and was completed around 1653. Court workshops produced miniature paintings, at their finest under Akbar and Jahangir. Your turn. Who wrote it?

en.title: The eighteenth century wasn't just decline

quiz.q: The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was fought between the Marathas and:
quiz.why: Right. Ahmad Shah Abdali.

en.transcript: After 1707, the Mughal empire weakened fast. But new regional states grew strong. Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739. The Marathas lost to Ahmad Shah Abdali at Panipat in 1761. Awadh, Bengal and Hyderabad broke away under former Mughal governors. The Marathas, the Sikhs and Mysore rose as new powers. Historians now stress regional prosperity, not just imperial collapse. Your turn. Against whom?

en.title: Britain and France fought for India in the Carnatic

quiz.q: The Battle of Wandiwash (1760) was fought between:
quiz.why: Right. The British and the French.

en.transcript: Before Britain ruled India, it had to beat France here. That happened in the Carnatic. Three Carnatic Wars ran from 1746 to 1763. The British victory at Wandiwash in 1760 ended French hopes. Dupleix led the French, and Robert Clive made his name for the British. The lesson: small, drilled European armies could decide who ruled Indian states. Your turn. Who fought at Wandiwash?

en.title: Two policies that swallowed Indian states

quiz.q: The Doctrine of Lapse is associated with:
quiz.why: Right. Lord Dalhousie.

en.transcript: The British didn't win every state by war. Some they took by treaty, others by inheritance rules. Under Lord Wellesley's subsidiary alliance, a ruler paid for British troops. He couldn't make other alliances, and accepted a British Resident. Hyderabad signed first. Under Lord Dalhousie, a state without a natural heir lapsed to the Company. Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur were annexed this way. Tipu Sultan refused. He was killed defending Seringapatam in 1799. Your turn. Who's associated with it?

en.title: Parliament began to rein in the Company in 1773

quiz.q: Who was the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act?
quiz.why: Right. Warren Hastings.

en.transcript: The East India Company ruled Bengal. But who controlled the Company? The Regulating Act of 1773 made Warren Hastings Governor-General of Bengal. A Supreme Court at Calcutta followed in 1774, and Pitt's India Act in 1784. Pitt's Act set up a Board of Control in London. The Court of Directors kept the commercial side. Every later Charter Act moved more power from the Company to Parliament. Your turn. Who was the first?

en.title: Naoroji showed how wealth flowed out of India

quiz.q: 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' was written by:
quiz.why: Right. Dadabhai Naoroji.

en.transcript: Was British rule good for India's economy? Dadabhai Naoroji added up the numbers. His Poverty and Un-British Rule in India was published in 1901. It argued that wealth was being drained to Britain. Home charges: salaries, pensions and interest paid in London. And exports that brought nothing back in return. Add deindustrialisation, which ruined handloom weavers, and commercial farming, linked to famines. Your turn. Who wrote it?

en.title: English education was planned in two documents

quiz.q: Which document is called the 'Magna Carta of English education in India'?
quiz.why: Right. Wood's Despatch, 1854.

en.transcript: How did English education spread in India? Two documents set the course. Macaulay's Minute of 1835 favoured English education. Wood's Despatch of 1854 set out a system, and three universities opened in 1857. Wood's Despatch is often called the Magna Carta of English education in India. The topic also covers the vernacular press, and the spread of modern science. Your turn. Which document?

en.title: Sati was banned in 1829, widow remarriage allowed in 1856

quiz.q: Sati was abolished in 1829 by:
quiz.why: Right. Lord William Bentinck.

en.transcript: Two reformers changed the law for Indian women. Ram Mohan Roy and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar. Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828. Sati was abolished in 1829, under Bentinck. Vidyasagar's campaign led to the Widow Remarriage Act in 1856. Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875. Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873. Note the method: reformers argued from both scripture and reason. Your turn. Who abolished sati?

en.title: Before 1857, peasants and tribes rose first

quiz.q: The play 'Nil Darpan' is about:
quiz.why: Right. The oppression of indigo cultivators.

en.transcript: 1857 is famous. But peasants and tribes had risen before, and after. The Santhals rose in 1855, led by Sidhu and Kanhu. Bengal's indigo farmers revolted in 1859. The Santhals fought moneylenders and land loss. Indigo farmers refused to grow the crop for planters. Dinabandhu Mitra's play Nil Darpan, in 1860, exposed the planters' cruelty. Your turn. What is it about?

en.title: Unfair laws helped unite Indian opinion

quiz.q: The Ilbert Bill (1883) concerned:
quiz.why: Right. Allowing Indian judges to try Europeans.

en.transcript: Sometimes, bad laws build nations. Two in particular angered educated Indians. Lord Lytton's Vernacular Press Act of 1878 muzzled Indian-language newspapers. The Ilbert Bill of 1883 tried to let Indian judges try Europeans, and was diluted after protests. Western education brought ideas of liberty. The press and the railways spread ideas faster. The Ilbert Bill row taught a lesson: Indians would not be treated as equals under the Raj. Your turn. What was it about?

en.title: Gandhi's first Indian satyagraha was for indigo farmers

quiz.q: Gandhi's first satyagraha in India was at:
quiz.why: Right. Champaran, 1917.

en.transcript: Gandhi's first satyagraha in India wasn't national. It was in a district in Bihar. In 1917, at Champaran, he took up the cause of indigo farmers. In 1918, he led peasants in Kheda, and mill workers in Ahmedabad. Satyagraha, non-violent resistance. And drawing peasants and workers into politics. In 1919, the Rowlatt Act triggered his first all-India protest. Your turn. Where was the first?

en.title: From councils to provincial autonomy

quiz.q: Dyarchy in the provinces was introduced by the Act of:
quiz.why: Right. The Government of India Act, 1919.

en.transcript: Step by step, the British let Indians into government. Each step came with limits. The 1909 Morley–Minto reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims. The 1919 Act brought dyarchy in the provinces. The 1935 Act gave provincial autonomy. Under dyarchy, some subjects were transferred to Indian ministers. Others were reserved for the Governor. The 1935 Act matters later too: much of our Constitution's administrative frame came from it. Your turn. Which Act?

en.title: Other strands: revolutionaries and the INA

quiz.q: The Azad Hind government was proclaimed in 1943 at:
quiz.why: Right. Singapore.

en.transcript: Not every freedom fighter followed non-violence. Two strands stand out. The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association was formed in 1928. Bhagat Singh was executed in 1931. Subhas Bose proclaimed the Azad Hind government in Singapore in 1943. Bhagat Singh wanted a socialist, secular republic. Bose sought armed struggle with foreign help. The Communist Party of India held its founding conference in 1925, at Kanpur. Your turn. Where was it proclaimed?

en.title: The road to partition, in three dates

quiz.q: The Lahore Resolution was passed in:
quiz.why: Right. March 1940.

en.transcript: Partition didn't happen overnight. Its political road ran over four decades. The Muslim League was founded at Dhaka in 1906. Its Lahore Resolution came in 1940. Partition followed in 1947. Separate electorates from 1909 hardened divisions. And the Cabinet Mission talks of 1946 failed. Write about it with care. Partition displaced millions, and cost many lives. Your turn. When was it passed?

en.title: Over 500 princely states joined India

quiz.q: Which three subjects did the Instrument of Accession first cover?
quiz.why: Right. Defence, external affairs and communications.

en.transcript: At independence, over 500 princely states had to choose. Almost all joined India peacefully. Sardar Patel led it as Home Minister, with V. P. Menon as secretary of the States Ministry. Junagadh joined after a plebiscite in 1948. Hyderabad was integrated after police action in September 1948. Rulers signed an Instrument of Accession, first ceding only defence, external affairs and communications. Your turn. Which three subjects?

en.title: Ambedkar turned to Buddhism in 1956

quiz.q: Which Article abolishes untouchability?
quiz.why: Right. Article 17.

en.transcript: The Constitution abolished untouchability. Ending it in practice took more. Article 17 abolished untouchability in 1950. A law to punish it followed in 1955. In October 1956, Ambedkar and lakhs of followers embraced Buddhism at Nagpur. The 1955 Act was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976. The topic also covers reservations, and ethnic movements after independence. Your turn. Which Article?

en.title: A walk asked landowners to give land away

quiz.q: The Bhoodan movement was started by:
quiz.why: Right. Vinoba Bhave, 1951.

en.transcript: Could land be redistributed without force? Vinoba Bhave tried asking for it. In 1951, at Pochampally, a landlord gave land to the landless at Vinoba Bhave's request. That began the Bhoodan movement. By law, zamindari was abolished in the early 1950s. Tenancy reforms and land ceilings had mixed results. The intermediaries went. But much of the inequality in land stayed. Your turn. Who started it?

en.title: Dare to know

quiz.q: The separation of powers is most associated with:
quiz.why: Right. Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws.

en.transcript: In 1784, Kant summed up an age in two words. Sapere aude. Dare to know. Kant said Enlightenment is leaving self-imposed immaturity. Thinking for yourself. Voltaire for tolerance. Rousseau for the general will. Montesquieu for the separation of powers. From here came liberalism, and later, socialism. Your turn. Who's associated with it?

en.title: No taxation without representation

quiz.q: The US Declaration of Independence was adopted in:
quiz.why: Right. 1776.

en.transcript: Thirteen colonies broke from Britain over taxes and rights. They wrote the first modern written constitution. The Declaration of Independence came in 1776. The US Constitution was written in 1787. The colonists' slogan: no taxation without representation. India borrowed ideas from it: a written constitution, judicial review, and a bill of rights. Your turn. When was it adopted?

en.title: Britain industrialised first, and fast

quiz.q: James Watt is known for:
quiz.why: Right. An improved steam engine.

en.transcript: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain? Coal, iron, capital, and colonies. Hargreaves's spinning jenny in the 1760s, and James Watt's improved steam engine, patented in 1769. Coal and iron close together. Capital, and markets, including colonies. The cost: long hours, child labour, and crowded, polluted cities. Your turn. What is Watt known for?

en.title: Modern states began with a peace treaty

quiz.q: German unification was completed in:
quiz.why: Right. 1871.

en.transcript: Where does the idea of sovereign states come from? Often, from a peace treaty in 1648. The Peace of Westphalia, in 1648, is linked to the idea of sovereign states. Italy was unified in 1861, and Germany in 1871. Cavour, Garibaldi and Mazzini in Italy. Bismarck in Germany, through blood and iron. Nationalism said one people should have one state. A powerful idea, and sometimes a dangerous one. Your turn. When was it completed?

en.title: Europe divided Africa at a conference table

quiz.q: The Berlin Conference (1884–85) was about:
quiz.why: Right. Rules for the European partition of Africa.

en.transcript: In 1884, European powers met in Berlin to set rules for claiming Africa. No Africans were present. The Berlin Conference opened in 1884. By 1914, nearly all of Africa was under European rule. Raw materials and markets. And prestige and strategy. The syllabus also covers colonialism in Asia and Latin America. Your turn. What was it about?

en.title: Two revolutions, 32 years apart

quiz.q: The People's Republic of China was proclaimed in:
quiz.why: Right. 1 October 1949.

en.transcript: The twentieth century's two great communist revolutions came in Russia, and in China. In 1917, the Bolsheviks took power in Russia. In 1949, Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China. In February, the Tsar fell. In October, Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power. Counter-revolution came too: fascism in Italy, and Nazism in Germany. Your turn. When was it proclaimed?

en.title: Two world wars in 31 years

quiz.q: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in:
quiz.why: Right. 1919.

en.transcript: Two world wars came within 31 years. India was drawn into both. The First World War began in 1914, after an assassination at Sarajevo. The Treaty of Versailles came in 1919. The Second War began in 1939. These were total wars: whole societies mobilised, and civilians targeted. Over a million Indian soldiers served in the First World War. The war's costs fed the national movement. Your turn. When was it signed?

en.title: The Cold War split the world into blocs

quiz.q: NATO was founded in:
quiz.why: Right. 1949.

en.transcript: After 1945, two superpowers faced off without fighting directly. The Cold War. The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan came in 1947. NATO in 1949. The Soviet bloc answered with the Warsaw Pact in 1955. The Berlin blockade, and the Cuban missile crisis of 1962. India's choice: non-alignment. Your turn. When was NATO founded?

en.title: Ghana led sub-Saharan Africa to freedom

quiz.q: Which was the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence (1957)?
quiz.why: Right. Ghana, 1957.

en.transcript: After 1945, empires that seemed permanent fell within decades. Asia first, then Africa. France lost Vietnam after Dien Bien Phu, in 1954. Ghana became the first sub-Saharan colony to win freedom, in 1957. South Africa's apartheid ended in 1994. Kwame Nkrumah in Ghana, and Nelson Mandela in South Africa. Latin America freed itself earlier, with leaders like Simón Bolívar. Your turn. Which country?

en.title: Underdevelopment was made, not found

quiz.q: 'How Europe Underdeveloped Africa' was written by:
quiz.why: Right. Walter Rodney.

en.transcript: Why did so many former colonies stay poor? Dependency theorists had an answer. Andre Gunder Frank wrote of the development of underdevelopment in 1966. Walter Rodney's How Europe Underdeveloped Africa followed in 1972. Rich core countries draw wealth from a poor periphery. Colonies were locked into exporting raw materials. Critics point to East Asia, which grew fast while trading with the West. Your turn. Who wrote it?

en.title: From coal and steel to a common currency

quiz.q: The European Economic Community was created by the:
quiz.why: Right. The Treaty of Rome, 1957.

en.transcript: Countries that fought two world wars built the world's deepest union. The Treaty of Rome created the European Economic Community in 1957. Maastricht created the EU in 1992. The euro launched in 1999. To keep the peace by tying economies together, and to prosper through a single market. Unity has limits: Britain left the EU in 2020. Your turn. Which treaty?

en.title: Openness and restructuring ended the USSR

quiz.q: Into how many countries did the USSR break up?
quiz.why: Right. 15.

en.transcript: In 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev tried to reform the Soviet Union. Six years later, it was gone. Glasnost meant openness. Perestroika meant restructuring the economy. The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, into 15 countries. The result: a unipolar moment, with the US as the only superpower, for a time. Your turn. Into how many countries?
